title: Heinrich events
summary: During the last ice age, between roughly 60,000 and 16,000 years ago, colossal armadas of icebergs periodically broke away from the Laurentide ice sheet and surged into the North Atlantic. As the icebergs melted, they deposited thick layers of ice-rafted debris across the seafloor and flooded the ocean with freshwater. These episodes, known as Heinrich events, disrupted the Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, cooling the subpolar North Atlantic and driving worldwide shifts in monsoons and polar temperatures.

uncertainty.note: Six major Heinrich events (H1 to H6) occurred between approximately 60,000 and 16,000 years ago, with the latest major event (H1) centered around 17,000–16,000 years ago (NSF; Martin et al. 2023; NOAA NCEI).

as_recorded.value: iceberg discharge events that are recorded in North Atlantic sediments

where.historical_name: Glacial North Atlantic Ocean, Late Pleistocene; no polities existed

importance.justification: Massive iceberg discharges disrupted Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, altering global atmospheric and oceanic climate patterns during the last glacial period.
